chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Nelson Mandela was the first black president of which country?
giai_thich: Nelson Mandela fought against the apartheid regime in South Africa, spending 27 years in prison. In 1994, during the first election where all citizens of every race could vote, he became president. He called for reconciliation instead of revenge. His birthday (July 18) is celebrated as International Nelson Mandela Day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the holiest city in Islam?
giai_thich: Mecca (Saudi Arabia) is the birthplace of the prophet Muhammad and home to the Kaaba, a cube-shaped structure covered in black cloth. Muslims around the world face Mecca when praying five times a day. Non-Muslims are not allowed to enter this city.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who is the prophet who founded Islam?
giai_thich: Muhammad was born around 570 in Mecca. According to Islam, from around 610 he received revelations from God (Allah) through the angel Gabriel. He died in 632 in Medina, by which time most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam. Today, Islam has nearly 2 billion followers, making it the second-largest religion in the world.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which sea does the Suez Canal connect to the Mediterranean?
giai_thich: The Suez Canal is approximately 193 km long, running through Egypt, connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. Thanks to the canal, ships traveling from Europe to Asia do not have to go around the southern tip of Africa, saving thousands of kilometers. About 12% of the world's trade goods pass through this canal.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which empire had its capital in Istanbul and ruled much of the Middle East for centuries?
giai_thich: The Ottoman Empire was founded by the Turks around 1299 and lasted over 600 years, until 1922. At its height, the empire stretched from Hungary to Iraq and from Algeria to the Arabian Peninsula. The name "Ottoman" comes from its founder, Osman I. The Byzantine Empire had its capital in the same city but fell in 1453.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the holy book of Islam called?
giai_thich: The Qur'an is written in Arabic and consists of 114 chapters (suras). Muslims believe this is the word of God revealed to Muhammad. Many people memorize the entire Qur'an, and such individuals are called "hafiz." The Torah is the holy book of Judaism, while the Vedas are ancient texts of Hinduism.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1948, which country was established in the Middle East?
giai_thich: On May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion declared the establishment of the state of Israel, one day before Britain ended its mandate over Palestine. The next day, neighboring Arab countries attacked, marking the beginning of the first Arab-Israeli war. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were displaced. The Israel-Palestine conflict continues to this day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the collection "One Thousand and One Nights," who tells stories to the king each night?
giai_thich: According to the tale, King Shahryar marries a new wife each day and has her killed the next morning. The clever Scheherazade tells stories each night but stops at the most exciting part, forcing the king to spare her life to hear the continuation. After 1001 nights, the king changes. Aladdin, Sinbad, and Ali Baba are characters in the stories she tells.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What was the system of racial segregation in South Africa (1948 – 1994) called?
giai_thich: Apartheid in Afrikaans means "separation." Laws divided people by skin color: black people could not vote, had to live in separate areas, attend separate schools, and even use separate park benches. This system was condemned and sanctioned by the world. Apartheid ended with the democratic elections in 1994.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Friday is the weekly prayer day for followers of which religion?
giai_thich: On Friday afternoons, male Muslim followers go to the mosque for communal prayers and sermons. Therefore, in many Muslim countries, the weekend is Friday and Saturday. The holy day for Jews is Saturday (Sabbath), while for Christians it is Sunday.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the name of the daytime fasting month for Muslims?
giai_thich: During the month of Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, believers refrain from eating and drinking from dawn until sunset to cultivate patience and empathy for the poor. Since the Islamic calendar is lunar, Ramadan occurs about 11 days earlier each year. The month concludes with the festival of Eid al-Fitr.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Where did the transatlantic slave trade primarily transport Africans?
giai_thich: From the 16th to the 19th century, about 12 million Africans were captured and shipped to America to work on sugar, cotton, and coffee plantations. Approximately 1.5 to 2 million died during the journey. Brazil received the most slaves. This is one of the greatest tragedies in human history.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the pilgrimage to Mecca that every eligible Muslim must perform at least once in their lifetime called?
giai_thich: Hajj is one of the five pillars of Islam, taking place in the last month of the Islamic calendar. Each year, about 2 million people from around the world go to Mecca, wearing the same white garments to symbolize equality among all. Zakat is the act of giving to the poor, which is also a pillar of Islam.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: How many years was Nelson Mandela imprisoned?
giai_thich: Mandela was arrested in 1962 and sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964. He was imprisoned until 1990, with the first 18 years spent in Robben Island prison, where he had to break rocks under the scorching sun. Upon his release at the age of 71, he bore no hatred and negotiated to peacefully end apartheid. The 18 years refers to his time on Robben Island, which can be confusing.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which city is the Western Wall (Wailing Wall), a sacred site for Jews, located?
giai_thich: The wall is a remnant of the wall surrounding the Second Temple of the Jews, destroyed by the Romans in 70 AD. Jews come here to pray and insert slips of paper with prayers into the cracks of the stones. Jerusalem is a holy city for all three religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the 1991 Gulf War, which country was liberated from Iraqi occupation by the coalition led by the United States?
giai_thich: In August 1990, Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait, a small oil-rich country. A coalition of about 35 nations launched an attack in January 1991 and liberated Kuwait in just about 100 hours of ground assault. Upon retreating, Iraqi forces set fire to approximately 700 oil wells, causing an environmental disaster.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Iraqi leader was overthrown in 2003?
giai_thich: Saddam Hussein ruled Iraq from 1979. In 2003, the U.S. and allies invaded Iraq under the pretext that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, which were never found. Saddam was captured while hiding in a bunker and was later tried and executed by an Iraqi court in 2006.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: On which peninsula did Islam originate?
giai_thich: Islam originated in the early 7th century in the Hejaz region, home to the cities of Mecca and Medina, on the Arabian Peninsula. Within about 100 years after Muhammad's death, Islam spread from Spain to India. The Arabian Peninsula is the largest peninsula in the world, mostly desert.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year was the Suez Canal inaugurated?
giai_thich: The canal was dug over 10 years (1859 – 1869), with the labor of tens of thousands of Egyptian workers, many of whom died from disease. The inauguration ceremony on November 17, 1869, was attended by French Empress Eugénie. 1914 was the year the Panama Canal was inaugurated, while 1956 was the year Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which leader ruled Libya for 42 years until he was overthrown in 2011?
giai_thich: Gaddafi came to power in 1969 through a coup at the age of 27. He was known for his unusual lifestyle, such as sleeping in a Bedouin tent while visiting foreign countries. In 2011, during the Arab Spring, uprisings erupted in Libya, and he was killed in October 2011.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The wave of protests known as the "Arab Spring" began in which country at the end of 2010?
giai_thich: On December 17, 2010, young vegetable vendor Mohamed Bouazizi self-immolated in protest against police confiscation of his cart. Protests spread across Tunisia, and just about a month later, President Ben Ali had to flee. The wave spread to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Syria, and many other countries. Tunisia was the only country that transitioned to a relatively stable democracy afterward.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did Muhammad's migration (Hijra) from Mecca to Medina, marking the beginning of the Islamic calendar, occur?
giai_thich: Facing opposition and threats from the Meccans, in 622 Muhammad and his followers moved to the city of Yathrib, later renamed Medina ("City of the Prophet"). Here he established the first Islamic community. The year 622 was chosen as year 1 of the Islamic calendar. The year 570 is when he was born, and 632 is when he died.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which colony is considered the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence from colonizers in 1957?
giai_thich: On March 6, 1957, the British colony of the Gold Coast gained independence and took the name Ghana, after an ancient empire in West Africa. Leader Kwame Nkrumah declared: "Ghana is forever free!" Ghana's independence inspired movements across Africa. Nigeria gained independence in 1960, and Kenya in 1963.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Before 1935, what name did the West use to refer to Iran?
giai_thich: Iranians have long referred to their country as Iran ("Land of the Aryans"). The name Persia comes from the province of Pars (Fars) in the south, the homeland of the ancient Persian kings. In 1935, Shah Reza Pahlavi suggested that countries use the name Iran. Mesopotamia refers to the region of Iraq, while Anatolia refers to Turkey.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What do Europeans call the numeral system 0, 1, 2, 3... that we use today?
giai_thich: This numeral system, including the number 0, was actually invented in India. Islamic mathematicians like al-Khwarizmi learned it and transmitted it to the Arab world, and then Europeans learned it back from them around the 12th-13th centuries. Therefore, Europeans refer to it as "Arabic numerals," while scientists call it Hindu-Arabic numerals.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did the Islamic Revolution overthrow Shah in Iran?
giai_thich: At the beginning of 1979, after months of protests by millions, King Mohammad Reza Pahlavi left the country. Religious leader Khomeini returned from Paris, and Iran became an Islamic Republic. The revolution profoundly changed Middle Eastern politics and Iran's relations with the West.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Besides Mecca, which city is considered the second holiest city in Islam?
giai_thich: Medina is where Muhammad lived his last years and is buried. The Prophet's mosque here is one of the largest mosques in the world. Jerusalem is considered the third holiest city in Islam, with the Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: "The House of Wisdom," a famous academic center during the golden age of Islam, was located in which city?
giai_thich: Under the Abbasid caliphs, around the 9th century, the House of Wisdom in Baghdad was where scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic while studying mathematics, astronomy, and medicine. As a result, many works of Aristotle and Euclid were preserved. The House of Wisdom was destroyed by the Mongols in 1258.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did Nelson Mandela become the president of South Africa?
giai_thich: On April 27, 1994, for the first time, South Africans of all colors were allowed to vote, with many waiting in line for hours. Mandela's ANC party won decisively, and he was inaugurated on May 10, 1994. 1990 was the year he was released from prison. He only served one term as president and voluntarily stepped down in 1999.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year was the Republic of Turkey, the successor state to the Ottoman Empire, declared?
giai_thich: After World War I, the Ottoman Empire was partitioned. Mustafa Kemal led the independence struggle, abolished the sultanate in 1922, and declared the Republic on October 29, 1923, with a new capital in Ankara instead of Istanbul. 1918 was the year the Ottomans were defeated in World War I.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which religious leader became the Supreme Leader of Iran after the 1979 revolution?
giai_thich: Ruhollah Khomeini was a Shia Muslim cleric who was exiled by the Shah in 1964. He lived in exile in Iraq and then France, sending recorded sermons back to Iran. After the revolution, he led Iran until his death in 1989. His successor was Ali Khamenei. "Ayatollah" is the title for a senior Shia cleric.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did the "Six-Day War" between Israel and Arab countries take place?
giai_thich: In June 1967, Israel launched a preemptive strike against Egypt, Syria, and Jordan. In just six days, Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank (including East Jerusalem), and the Golan Heights, increasing its territory by about three times. The war left territorial issues that remain disputed to this day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The island of Gorée off the coast of Senegal is famous as a symbol of what?
C: The capital of the Mali Empire
giai_thich: The island features the "House of Slaves" with the "Door of No Return," believed to be where Africans were taken aboard ships to America. Historians debate the actual number of people who passed through here, but the island has become an important memorial. Many U.S. presidents and popes have visited. Gorée Island is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which African country has never been a colony, only briefly occupied by Italy from 1936 to 1941?
giai_thich: Ethiopia defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 and maintained its independence during the European scramble for Africa. In 1935-1936, Mussolini's fascist Italy invaded and occupied, but Ethiopia was liberated in 1941 with British assistance. Thus, the green, yellow, and red of the Ethiopian flag became a symbol of independence for many African countries.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who led Ghana to independence and became its first president?
giai_thich: Kwame Nkrumah studied in the U.S. and the U.K. He organized nonviolent strikes and protests, was imprisoned, and won elections while still in prison. He aimed to unify all of Africa and initiated the Organization of African Unity. In 1966, he was overthrown while visiting China.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Liberia, a country in West Africa, was founded by freed slaves from which country?
giai_thich: From 1822, the American Colonization Society transported free black people from the U.S. to establish a settlement in West Africa. In 1847, Liberia ("Land of the Free") declared independence, becoming the first republic in Africa. The capital, Monrovia, is named after U.S. President James Monroe, and the Liberian flag closely resembles the U.S. flag.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Al-Qarawiyyin University, considered the oldest active university in the world, is located in which country?
giai_thich: Al-Qarawiyyin was founded in 859 in the city of Fez by Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a wealthy merchant. This is a rare example of a woman founding a major educational institution in the medieval period. According to the Guinness World Records, it is the oldest existing degree-granting university in the world. Al-Azhar University in Cairo was established about 100 years later.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the first Prime Minister and then President of independent Kenya?
giai_thich: Jomo Kenyatta was imprisoned by the British government for about 9 years for allegedly leading the Mau Mau uprising, although he always denied it. Kenya gained independence on December 12, 1963, and he led the country until his death in 1978. His famous slogan was "Harambee," meaning "Let us all pull together." His son, Uhuru Kenyatta, later also became president.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1993, Nelson Mandela jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize with which South African president?
giai_thich: Frederik Willem de Klerk was the last white president of South Africa. In 1990, he unexpectedly released Mandela from prison, allowed the ANC to operate again, and began negotiations to end apartheid. The two jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 for peacefully transitioning South Africa to democracy. De Klerk later served as vice president under Mandela.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Egyptian president nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956?
giai_thich: Nasser came to power after the revolution in 1952. When the U.S. and Britain withdrew their loan for the construction of the Aswan Dam, he nationalized the Suez Canal to collect tolls. Britain, France, and Israel attacked Egypt but had to withdraw under pressure from the U.S. and the Soviet Union. Nasser became a hero of the Arab world.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1871, which journalist found explorer David Livingstone in Africa and exclaimed the famous phrase "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?"
giai_thich: Livingstone was a Scottish missionary and explorer who lost contact with the outside world for many years while searching for the source of the Nile River. The New York Herald sent journalist Stanley to find him. They met in Ujiji, by Lake Tanganyika. Stanley's overly polite greeting in the wilderness became a famous saying.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which African king is often considered the richest in history, famous for his pilgrimage laden with gold in 1324?
giai_thich: Mansa Musa was the emperor of the Mali Empire, which had some of the largest gold mines in the world at that time. On his way to Mecca, his pilgrimage was said to have thousands of people and dozens of camels carrying gold, and he distributed gold everywhere he passed. The journey made the Mediterranean world aware of Mali, and he appeared on the 1375 Catalan map holding a gold nugget.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The subject "algebra" is named after the book of which Islamic mathematician?
giai_thich: Muhammad al-Khwarizmi worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad in the 9th century. His book contains the word "al-jabr" (meaning "restoration") in its title, from which the term "algebra" is derived. His name in Latin is written as "Algoritmi", which is where the term "algorithm" used by computers today comes from.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Egyptian president signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1979 and was assassinated in 1981?
giai_thich: Sadat was the president after Nasser. In 1977, he unexpectedly flew to Jerusalem and spoke before the Israeli Parliament, being the first Arab leader to do so. Egypt became the first Arab country to recognize Israel, in exchange for Israel returning the Sinai Peninsula. Many opposed this, and in 1981 he was assassinated during a parade.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Battle of Adwa in 1896, Ethiopia defeated the army of which country?
giai_thich: Emperor Menelik II assembled about 100,000 troops armed with modern weapons and defeated the Italian army near the town of Adwa. This was the first time in modern history that an African army completely defeated a European power. Italy had to recognize Ethiopia's independence. March 2nd is celebrated as Adwa Victory Day in Ethiopia.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the last emperor of Ethiopia?
giai_thich: Haile Selassie reigned from 1930 to 1974. In 1936, he addressed the League of Nations, calling for the world to help Ethiopia against Italian fascism, but was not responded to. In 1974, he was overthrown by a group of military officers and died in 1975. Traditionally, Ethiopian emperors claim descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who founded the Mali Empire in West Africa in the 13th century?
giai_thich: According to the oral epic of the Mandinka people, Sundiata was crippled as a child and could not walk, but grew up to become a fierce warrior. Around 1235, he defeated the sorcerer king Sumanguru and established the Mali Empire. The story has been passed down by griots for over 700 years, and he is also said to have issued a charter on the rights and duties of the people.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The city of Timbuktu, a famous center of Islamic scholarship and trade in the Middle Ages, is located in which modern-day country?
giai_thich: Timbuktu is located near the Niger River, where caravans carrying salt from the Sahara Desert met boats carrying gold from the south. In the 15th and 16th centuries, the city had many schools and tens of thousands of handwritten manuscripts. In English, "from here to Timbuktu" once meant "very far away". In 2012, many residents risked their lives to hide ancient manuscripts to protect them from destruction.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which empire replaced Mali as the largest empire in West Africa in the 15th and 16th centuries?
giai_thich: Songhai had its capital in Gao, by the Niger River. Under the reigns of Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad, the empire controlled Timbuktu and became one of the largest empires in African history. In 1591, Moroccan troops armed with firearms crossed the Sahara Desert to attack, leading to the collapse of Songhai.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Modern Ghana takes its name from an ancient empire. Where was the ancient Ghana Empire located?
giai_thich: The ancient Ghana Empire (around the 4th to 13th centuries) was famous for its wealth in gold, located about 700 to 800 km northwest of present-day Ghana. When the Gold Coast gained independence in 1957, Nkrumah chose the name Ghana to evoke Africa's glorious past. "Ghana" was originally a title for the king, meaning "warrior king."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the name of the largest stone city in sub-Saharan Africa, which has given its name to a country?
giai_thich: Great Zimbabwe was built from around the 11th to 15th centuries using stacked granite stones without mortar, featuring walls approximately 11 meters high. It was once a center for gold trade with Indian Ocean merchants. During colonial times, some Europeans doubted that Africans could have built this structure. Upon independence in 1980, Rhodesia was renamed Zimbabwe ("House of Stone").

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which ancient kingdom in Ethiopia was one of the first states in the world to adopt Christianity as its state religion?
giai_thich: The Kingdom of Aksum became wealthy through trade across the Red Sea and even minted its own gold coins. Around 330, King Ezana converted to Christianity, well ahead of many European nations. Aksum is famous for its giant stone obelisks, some over 20 meters tall. Ethiopians believe the Ark of the Covenant from the Bible is kept in a church in Aksum.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which country are the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela located?
giai_thich: In the 12th to 13th centuries, King Lalibela commissioned the carving of 11 churches from solid rock, excavated from top to bottom, to create a "New Jerusalem" for pilgrims. Each church was carved from a single block of stone, complete with windows, columns, and roofs. The churches are still used for worship today and are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who founded the powerful Zulu Kingdom in southern Africa in the early 19th century?
giai_thich: Shaka reformed the Zulu army: replacing long throwing spears with short stabbing spears, using large shields, and employing a "horns of the buffalo" formation to encircle enemies. He transformed the small Zulu tribe into a powerful kingdom. In 1828, he was assassinated by his half-brothers, including Dingane. Cetshwayo was the later Zulu king who fought against the British.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Battle of Isandlwana in 1879, the Zulu army defeated the army of which nation?
giai_thich: On January 22, 1879, about 20,000 Zulu warriors armed only with spears and shields annihilated a British force equipped with modern rifles, killing over 1,300 men. This was one of the heaviest defeats of the British army during the colonial era. However, a few months later, the British defeated the Zulu and captured King Cetshwayo.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Boer War in South Africa was a conflict between the British and whom?
giai_thich: The Boers (or Afrikaners) are descendants of Dutch, German, and French settlers in South Africa. When gold was discovered in their territory, the British sought to control it and went to war (1899 – 1902). The British placed Boer civilians in concentration camps, where about 26,000 women and children died. The British won, and in 1910, the Union of South Africa was established.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which British colony was named after the capitalist Cecil Rhodes?
giai_thich: Cecil Rhodes made his fortune from diamond mines, founded the De Beers company, and served as Prime Minister of the Cape Colony. His company seized land that was named Rhodesia. Northern Rhodesia is now Zambia, while Southern Rhodesia is now Zimbabwe. He left a legacy by establishing the Rhodes Scholarship at Oxford University, which still exists today.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which colony did King Leopold II of Belgium personally own as his private property?
giai_thich: From 1885 to 1908, the "Congo Free State" was the personal property of Leopold II, not of Belgium. The people were forced to harvest rubber, and those who did not meet quotas could have their hands cut off. Millions died. When these atrocities were exposed, Leopold was forced to cede Congo to the Belgian state in 1908.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did Algeria gain independence from France?
giai_thich: France ruled Algeria from 1830 and considered it part of its territory, with about 1 million European settlers. The war for independence (1954 – 1962) was extremely brutal. After a referendum, Algeria gained independence on July 5, 1962. Algeria is now the largest country in Africa.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Traditionally, around what year was the prophet Muhammad born?
giai_thich: Muhammad was born in Mecca, belonging to the Quraysh tribe. His father died before he was born, and his mother passed away when he was about 6 years old, so he was raised by his grandfather and then his uncle. Growing up, he worked as a trader with caravans and became known for his honesty, earning the nickname "al-Amin" (the trustworthy).

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the first caliph (successor) of Muhammad?
giai_thich: Abu Bakr was a close friend and father-in-law of Muhammad, one of the earliest followers of Islam. After Muhammad's death in 632, the community chose him as caliph ("successor"). He ruled for about 2 years, uniting the Arabian Peninsula. He, Umar, Uthman, and Ali are referred to by Sunnis as the four "Rightly Guided Caliphs."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who do Shia Muslims believe is the rightful successor of Muhammad?
giai_thich: Ali was Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, the husband of his daughter Fatimah. Shia Muslims (from "Shiat Ali", meaning "party of Ali") believe that Muhammad appointed Ali as his successor. Sunnis accept the community's choice of Abu Bakr. Today, about 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, while Shia are the majority in Iran and Iraq.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Where did the Umayyad dynasty, the first hereditary caliphate, establish its capital?
giai_thich: In 661, Muawiya established the Umayyad dynasty and chose Damascus (Syria) as its capital. Under the Umayyads, the Islamic empire stretched from Spain to Central Asia, becoming one of the largest empires in history. The Umayyad Mosque in Damascus is one of the oldest mosques in the world. In 750, the Umayyad dynasty was overthrown by the Abbasids.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which dynasty built the city of Baghdad in 762?
giai_thich: Caliph al-Mansur of the Abbasid dynasty built Baghdad on the Tigris River in a perfect circular shape, with the palace and mosque at the center, hence it was called the "Round City." Within a few decades, Baghdad became one of the largest cities in the world. This is the backdrop for many stories in "One Thousand and One Nights."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The traveler Ibn Battuta, who traveled about 120,000 km in the 14th century, was from where?
giai_thich: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier (Morocco). In 1325, at the age of 21, he set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca and continued traveling for nearly 30 years, reaching East Africa, India, Southeast Asia, and China. His journey was about three times that of Marco Polo. Upon returning home, he dictated his travels into a book called "Rihla" (Journey).

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which work is Ibn Sina (Avicenna) most famous for?
giai_thich: Ibn Sina (980 – 1037) was Persian. He memorized the Qur'an by age 10 and practiced medicine from ages 16 to 18. The Canon of Medicine consists of 5 volumes, compiling medical knowledge from Greek, Persian, and Indian sources. This book was used as a textbook in European medical schools for about 600 years.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Sultan Saladin, who recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, established which dynasty?
giai_thich: Saladin was Kurdish and served under the Syrian lords. In 1171, he ended the Fatimid dynasty in Egypt and established the Ayyubid dynasty, named after his father Ayyub. This dynasty ruled Egypt, Syria, and parts of Iraq and Yemen. In 1250, the Ayyubid dynasty was overthrown by its own Mamluk slave army.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which force first halted the Mongol army at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260?
giai_thich: After capturing Baghdad and Damascus, the Mongol army advanced towards Egypt. At Ain Jalut ("Spring of Goliath", in Palestine), the Mamluks lured the Mongols into a trap and defeated them. This was the first major defeat of the Mongols on the battlefield from which they could not take revenge, saving Egypt and the Islamic holy sites in the Arabian Peninsula.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which religion did the Safavid Empire in Persia choose as its state religion?
giai_thich: When the Safavid dynasty was established in 1501, Shah Ismail I declared Shia Islam as the state religion, even though at that time the majority of Persians were Sunni. This helped Persia develop a distinct identity, different from the Sunni Ottoman Empire to the west. Thus, today Iran is the center of Shia Islam.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which city was the capital of Persia during Shah Abbas's reign, praised as "half the world"?
giai_thich: In 1598, Shah Abbas the Great moved the capital to Isfahan and built Naqsh-e Jahan Square, one of the largest squares in the world, surrounded by beautiful blue-tiled mosques and a market. The Persians have a saying, "Isfahan nesf-e jahan", meaning "Isfahan is half the world."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The secret Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916 divided the Ottoman region of the Middle East into spheres of influence, signed between Britain and which country?
giai_thich: British diplomat Mark Sykes and French diplomat François Georges-Picot outlined the borders: Britain controlled Iraq, Jordan, and Palestine, while France controlled Syria and Lebanon. Russia was also informed and agreed. After the October Revolution of 1917, the Bolshevik government announced the agreement, causing Arabs to feel betrayed.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Balfour Declaration of 1917, supporting the establishment of a "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine, was issued by which government?
giai_thich: British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote a short letter to Lord Rothschild, a leader of the Jewish community in Britain. The letter promised support for a homeland for the Jews in Palestine while not prejudicing the rights of other communities there. At the same time, Britain also made promises to the Arabs, and these conflicting promises contributed to long-term conflict.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The British officer known as "Lawrence of Arabia" assisted the Arab revolt against which empire?
giai_thich: T. E. Lawrence was an archaeologist who became an intelligence officer. He dressed in Arab clothing and, alongside Prince Faisal, led guerrilla attacks on the Ottoman Hejaz railway and captured the port of Aqaba in 1917. His story was adapted into the classic film that won 7 Oscars in 1962.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the first Prime Minister of Israel?
giai_thich: Ben-Gurion was born in Poland and immigrated to Palestine in 1906. He was the one who proclaimed the establishment of the state of Israel in 1948 and served as Prime Minister for most of the time from 1948 to 1963. In his later years, he lived in an agricultural settlement (kibbutz) in the Negev desert. The main international airport in Israel is named after him.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who is considered the founder of modern Zionism?
giai_thich: Theodor Herzl was an Austro-Hungarian journalist. Witnessing the wave of anti-Semitism in Europe, he wrote "The Jewish State" in 1896 and organized the First Zionist Congress in 1897 in Basel (Switzerland). He died in 1904, about 44 years before the state of Israel was established. Chaim Weizmann was the first president of Israel.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Yom Kippur War, when Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel, occurred in which year?
giai_thich: On October 6, 1973, the holiest day of Yom Kippur for Jews, Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal and Syrian troops attacked the Golan Heights. Israel was caught off guard but later counterattacked. The war led to an oil embargo by Arab nations, causing a global energy crisis.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Camp David Accords of 1978 between Egypt and Israel were mediated by which U.S. president?
giai_thich: President Carter invited Egyptian President Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Begin to Camp David, the U.S. presidential retreat, and negotiated for 13 days. At times, the two leaders were reluctant to meet, and Carter had to shuttle between them. The agreement led to the Egypt-Israel peace treaty in 1979.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Oslo Accords of 1993, which Palestinian leader did Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin shake hands with in a historic moment?
giai_thich: After secret negotiations in Norway, Rabin and Arafat, the leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), shook hands in front of the White House with President Clinton standing in between. The two sides recognized each other for the first time, and the Palestinians were granted self-governance in part of the territory. Rabin, Arafat, and Shimon Peres jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Israeli Prime Minister was assassinated by an extremist Israeli in 1995?
giai_thich: On November 4, 1995, after speaking at a peace rally in Tel Aviv, Rabin was shot dead by an extremist Jewish student who opposed the Oslo Accords. Rabin had previously been the Chief of Staff during the Six-Day War and later became a peace advocate. The square where he was assassinated is now named after him.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who founded the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932?
giai_thich: In 1902, Abdulaziz Ibn Saud, along with a few dozen men, launched a surprise attack and recaptured Riyadh, his ancestral city. Over the next 30 years, he conquered most of the Arabian Peninsula, including Mecca and Medina, and named the country after his family as "Saudi Arabia." He had about 100 children, and subsequent Saudi kings are all his descendants.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When was oil first discovered with commercial reserves in Saudi Arabia?
giai_thich: American engineers drilled many unsuccessful wells until Dammam No. 7, where oil finally gushed out in March 1938 after nearly two years of drilling. This discovery transformed a poor kingdom in the desert into one of the richest countries in the world. 1908 was the year oil was first found in Persia (Iran).

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which city was the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) founded in 1960?
giai_thich: OPEC was established at a conference in Baghdad with five founding members: Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela. The goal was for oil-producing countries to control oil prices together instead of letting Western oil companies decide. OPEC's headquarters was initially in Geneva, then moved to Vienna (Austria) in 1965.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What measure did Arab oil-exporting countries take in 1973 that caused a global energy crisis?
D: Impose an oil embargo on the US and its allies
giai_thich: In protest against the US and some countries supporting Israel during the Yom Kippur War, Arab countries stopped selling oil to them and cut production. Oil prices increased about fourfold in just a few months. In the US, people had to wait in long lines to buy gasoline, and many European countries banned driving on Sundays.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the last king (Shah) of Iran?
giai_thich: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi ascended to the throne in 1941 at the age of 21, after his father was forced to abdicate by the British and Soviets. He modernized Iran in a Western style but ruled autocratically, with a feared secret police. In 1979, he had to leave Iran and died in Egypt in 1980. His father, Reza Shah, founded the Pahlavi dynasty.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: How many days did the hostage crisis at the US Embassy in Tehran (1979 – 1981) last?
giai_thich: In November 1979, Iranian students seized the US Embassy and held 52 Americans hostage, demanding the US return the Shah to Iran for trial. A rescue mission in 1980 ended in disaster. The hostages were released after 444 days, on the day President Reagan took office. The number 52 refers to the hostages, not the number of days.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Iran-Iraq War, one of the longest wars of the 20th century, lasted from when to when?
giai_thich: In September 1980, Saddam Hussein attacked Iran, hoping for a quick victory while Iran was in chaos after the revolution. The war turned into a trench warfare similar to World War I, involving chemical weapons. About half a million people or more died, but when the ceasefire was declared in 1988, the borders of the two countries remained almost unchanged.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What was the name of the military operation by the coalition to liberate Kuwait in 1991?
giai_thich: From August 1990, the coalition deployed forces to Saudi Arabia in Operation Desert Shield for defense. On January 17, 1991, the offensive operation Desert Storm began with large-scale airstrikes, broadcast live around the world. "Iraqi Freedom" is the name of the operation to attack Iraq in 2003.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which city was once called the "Paris of the Middle East" before being devastated by the civil war from 1975 to 1990?
giai_thich: Beirut, the capital of Lebanon, was once a bustling center of banking, tourism, and culture, with a lifestyle blending French and Arab influences. Lebanon has many religious communities (Christian, Sunni Muslim, Shia, Druze), and the fragile balance among them broke down in 1975. The civil war lasted 15 years, resulting in about 150,000 deaths.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which country did King Hussein rule for nearly 47 years, from 1952 to 1999?
giai_thich: Hussein became king of Jordan at the age of 17, after witnessing his grandfather's assassination in Jerusalem. He survived numerous assassination attempts and signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994. He was also a pilot, race car driver, and amateur radio operator. His son, King Abdullah II, succeeded him in 1999.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The United Arab Republic (1958 – 1961) was a merger between Egypt and which country?
giai_thich: In 1958, Syrian leaders proposed a merger with Nasser's Egypt, who was a symbol of Arab nationalism. Nasser became president, and the capital was set in Cairo. However, the Syrians gradually became dissatisfied as they felt dominated by Egypt, and in 1961 a coup in Damascus led to Syria's separation. Egypt kept this name until 1971.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Ottoman Sultan conquered Egypt during the Mamluk period in 1517?
giai_thich: Selim I (nicknamed "Selim the Grim") ruled for only 8 years but nearly doubled the Ottoman territory. He defeated the Safavid dynasty in 1514, then conquered Syria and Egypt from the Mamluks in 1516 – 1517. From then on, the Ottoman sultans controlled Mecca and Medina and claimed the title of caliph of the Islamic world. His son was Suleiman the Magnificent.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1924, which title, considered the leader of the entire Sunni Muslim world, was abolished by the Turkish Parliament?
giai_thich: After abolishing the sultanate in 1922, Turkey still retained a symbolic caliph. In March 1924, Mustafa Kemal abolished the caliphate and expelled the entire Ottoman family from the country. The caliphate had existed for about 1,300 years, since the time of Abu Bakr. Shah is the title of the king of Persia.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What was the elite infantry force of the Ottoman Empire, originally consisting of Christian boys taken for training, called?
giai_thich: Under the devshirme system, boys from Christian villages in the Balkans were taken, converted to Islam, and rigorously trained. They became the loyal bodyguards of the sultan, the first standing army in Europe since Roman times. Their marching music (mehter) is one of the oldest military music types in the world. Sipahi refers to Ottoman cavalry.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Muhammad Ali Pasha, regarded as the "father of modern Egypt," belonged to which ethnic background?
giai_thich: Muhammad Ali was born in Kavala (now part of Greece) to an Albanian family. He arrived in Egypt in 1801 with the Ottoman army to fight the French and became the ruler of Egypt in 1805. He built factories, canals, schools, and a modern European-style army, and cultivated cotton for export. His dynasty ruled Egypt until 1952.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did Napoleon Bonaparte invade Egypt?
giai_thich: Napoleon aimed to seize Egypt to cut off the route from Britain to India. He defeated the Mamluk forces, but his fleet was destroyed by Nelson at the Battle of Abukir, leaving the French stranded. He brought along about 160 scientists and artists to study Egypt. Their work, "Description of Egypt," sparked an Egyptology craze in Europe.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which French engineer-diplomat was responsible for constructing the Suez Canal?
giai_thich: Ferdinand de Lesseps was a diplomat rather than a trained engineer, but he convinced the ruler of Egypt and established a company to build the canal. After the success at Suez, he attempted to build the Panama Canal in 1881 but failed due to malaria, yellow fever, and difficult terrain, resulting in the deaths of tens of thousands of workers. Gustave Eiffel was also involved and was implicated in the Panama scandal.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1875, under which Prime Minister did Britain purchase shares in Egypt's Suez Canal?
giai_thich: The ruler of Egypt, Ismail Pasha, was heavily in debt and had to sell shares in the Suez Canal. Disraeli quickly purchased them for £4 million, borrowing money from the Rothschild bank without waiting for Parliament's approval. He wrote to Queen Victoria: "Dear Queen, it is yours." The Suez Canal became the "lifeline" connecting Britain to India.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: During the Suez Crisis of 1956, which country, along with Britain and France, attacked Egypt?
giai_thich: Britain, France, and Israel secretly agreed: Israel would attack the Sinai Peninsula first, then Britain and France would send troops under the pretext of "separating the two sides." The US was very angry for not being informed in advance and, along with the Soviet Union, pressured the three countries to withdraw. The crisis demonstrated that Britain and France were no longer superpowers, and for the first time, the United Nations sent peacekeeping forces.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the leader that led the Algerian people in their resistance against French colonialism and became the first president of independent Algeria in 1962?
giai_thich: Ahmed Ben Bella was one of the founding leaders of the National Liberation Front of Algeria (FLN). After the Évian Accords in 1962 ended over a century of French rule, he was elected the first president of the country. Algeria's struggle for independence is one of the most heroic and fierce chapters in the decolonization movement in Africa.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which king of Saudi Arabia is famous for implementing the oil embargo in 1973 and promoting modernization in the country before being assassinated in 1975?
giai_thich: King Faisal bin Abdulaziz Al Saud ascended the throne in 1964 and led the country through a period of remarkable development thanks to enormous oil revenues. During the Arab-Israeli War in 1973, he initiated the decision to cut production and impose an oil embargo, shaking the Western economy. Unfortunately, he died after being assassinated by a cousin at the palace.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: By 1914, apart from Ethiopia, which African country managed to maintain its independence?
giai_thich: During the "Scramble for Africa," European countries divided almost the entire continent among themselves. Only Ethiopia (thanks to its victory at Adwa) and Liberia (due to its special relationship with the U.S.) managed to remain independent. Egypt was a protectorate of Britain, Morocco was divided between France and Spain in 1912, and South Africa was a self-governing territory of the British Empire.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Patrice Lumumba was the first prime minister of which country?
giai_thich: Lumumba was a postal worker who became the independence leader of Belgian Congo. During the independence ceremony on June 30, 1960, he delivered a fierce speech about the injustices of colonial rule right in front of the Belgian king. Just a few months later, he was overthrown, and in early 1961, he was assassinated. He became a symbol of the anti-colonial movement in Africa.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1971, the dictator Mobutu Sese Seko renamed the Congo to what?
giai_thich: Mobutu came to power in 1965 and implemented the policy of "authenticité": renaming the country, the Congo River, and cities to African names, and forbidding the use of Christian names. He ruled for 32 years and amassed enormous wealth while the country remained impoverished. In 1997, he was overthrown, and the country reclaimed the name Democratic Republic of the Congo.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Julius Nyerere, known as "Mwalimu" (Teacher), was the leader of which country?
giai_thich: Nyerere was a teacher who led Tanganyika to a peaceful independence in 1961. He proposed the "Ujamaa" (familyhood) policy, establishing collective villages and using Swahili as a common language, helping to unite over 120 ethnic groups. He also translated two of Shakespeare's plays into Swahili. He voluntarily stepped down from the presidency in 1985.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1964, Tanganyika merged with which island to form Tanzania?
giai_thich: The name Tanzania is a combination of "Tanganyika" and "Zanzibar." Zanzibar was an archipelago famous for its cloves and was a center for the slave trade in East Africa under the Omani sultans. Pemba is an island that is part of the Zanzibar archipelago, so it is not the answer. Singer Freddie Mercury of the band Queen was born in Zanzibar.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The shortest war in history, lasting only about 38 – 45 minutes in 1896, occurred between Britain and which country?
giai_thich: When the pro-British sultan of Zanzibar died, another person ascended the throne without British consent. Britain issued an ultimatum, and when it expired, British warships bombarded the palace. After about 40 minutes, the palace caught fire, the flag was shot down, and the sultan fled. This is recorded in the history books as the shortest war in history.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Idi Amin was the notorious dictator of which country in the 1970s?
giai_thich: Idi Amin was a former boxer and officer in the British colonial army. He staged a coup in 1971 and ruled with an iron fist, causing hundreds of thousands of deaths. In 1972, he expelled about 80,000 Asians from Uganda. In 1979, he was overthrown by Tanzanian forces and exiled Ugandans, living in exile in Saudi Arabia until his death.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1994, a genocide that resulted in approximately 800,000 deaths in about 100 days occurred in which country?
giai_thich: After the plane carrying the Rwandan president was shot down, extremist Hutu groups massacred Tutsis and moderate Hutus. The world almost did not intervene. The genocide ended when the Rwandan Patriotic Front took control of the country. Today, Rwanda has significantly recovered and has one of the highest rates of female parliamentary representation in the world.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: South Sudan, the most recently recognized country by the United Nations, separated from Sudan and gained independence in which year?
giai_thich: After two civil wars lasting nearly 40 years between the north (predominantly Muslim, Arabic-speaking) and the south, in 2011, the people of South Sudan voted in a referendum with about 99% choosing independence. The new country was born on July 9, 2011, with Juba as its capital. The year 2005 was when the peace agreement was signed, paving the way for the referendum.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in which year?
giai_thich: Eritrea was once an Italian colony, later annexed by Ethiopia in 1962. The Eritreans fought for about 30 years, achieving military victory in 1991 and officially gaining independence after a referendum in 1993. This caused Ethiopia to lose its entire coastline and become a landlocked country. From 1998 to 2000, the two countries fought a border war.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: During the Nigerian Civil War (1967 – 1970), which region declared independence?
giai_thich: The Igbo people in southeastern Nigeria declared the Republic of Biafra in 1967. The government forces blockaded the region, causing a terrible famine that resulted in approximately 1 to 2 million deaths. Images of malnourished Biafran children shocked the world, and Médecins Sans Frontières was founded from the experience of providing aid here. Katanga is a secessionist region in Congo.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Mau Mau uprising against British colonialism (1952 – 1960) took place in which country?
giai_thich: The Kikuyu people in the Kenyan highlands were dispossessed of fertile land by white settlers. They formed the armed Mau Mau movement. The British government suppressed it very violently, detaining tens of thousands of people in camps. In 2013, the British government officially expressed regret and compensated thousands of surviving victims.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The largest Portuguese colony in Africa, which gained independence in 1975, is which country?
giai_thich: Portugal was the first European country to arrive in Africa and also the last to leave. Angola is about 14 times larger than Portugal and is rich in oil and diamonds. After gaining independence on November 11, 1975, Angola fell into a civil war that lasted until 2002. Mozambique also gained independence in 1975 but is smaller than Angola.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Zimbabwe (formerly Rhodesia) officially gained internationally recognized independence in which year?
giai_thich: In 1965, the white minority government of Ian Smith unilaterally declared Rhodesia independent from Britain to maintain control, but almost no country recognized it. After many years of guerrilla warfare, an election involving all citizens was held, and Zimbabwe gained independence on April 18, 1980. The year 1965 is therefore a confusing option.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Africa Day (May 25) commemorates the founding of which organization in 1963?
D: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
giai_thich: On May 25, 1963, leaders of 32 independent African countries met in Addis Ababa and established the Organization of African Unity to eliminate colonialism and promote unity. In 2002, the OAU was replaced by the African Union (AU), which currently has 55 members. Since the AU emerged from the OAU, the AU option can be misleading.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Where is the headquarters of the African Union located?
giai_thich: Addis Ababa (Ethiopia) was chosen because Ethiopia symbolizes African independence and Emperor Haile Selassie was a strong advocate for the establishment of the OAU. The current headquarters of the AU is a skyscraper built with funding from China, inaugurated in 2012. The city also hosts the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which South African Archbishop received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 for his nonviolent struggle against apartheid?
giai_thich: Desmond Tutu is famous for his radiant smile and humor, but he was very determined against injustice. He coined the term "Rainbow Nation" to refer to a multi-ethnic South Africa. After 1994, he chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, where victims and perpetrators of crimes under apartheid recounted the truth. He passed away in 2021.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Sharpeville massacre in 1960, when police shot at protesters opposing the "pass laws," occurred in which country?
giai_thich: The pass laws required black people to carry permits to be in white areas. On March 21, 1960, police opened fire on a crowd of protesters in Sharpeville, killing 69 people. Subsequently, the ANC was banned and shifted to armed struggle. March 21 is now Human Rights Day in South Africa and International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What did the Soweto uprising of 1976 in South Africa protest against?
giai_thich: The apartheid government mandated that half of the subjects be taught in Afrikaans, a language that black students considered the language of the oppressor. On June 16, 1976, thousands of students took to the streets to protest, and police opened fire. The image of 13-year-old Hector Pieterson dying became iconic. June 16 is now Youth Day in South Africa.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Nelson Mandela spent most of his prison time on which island?
giai_thich: Robben Island, located off the coast of Cape Town, was once a political prison. Mandela spent 18 years here in a small cell measuring about 2 by 2.5 meters, sleeping on a thin mat and working in a limestone quarry, with bright light damaging his eyes. Prisoners secretly organized study sessions, so the island was jokingly referred to as "Mandela University." The island is now a museum and a World Heritage site.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Elmina Castle in Ghana, the oldest European structure in sub-Saharan Africa and once a slave trading post, was built by whom in 1482?
giai_thich: The Portuguese built Elmina ("Gold Mine") to trade gold, and it later became a holding station for slaves before they were shipped to the Americas. In 1637, the Dutch captured the castle. Today, visitors can see the dark dungeons and the "Door of No Return." The castle is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Kingdom of Benin (now part of Nigeria) is famous for its artworks made from what material?
giai_thich: Thousands of relief panels and statues made of bronze, brass, and ivory decorated the palace of the Benin king, depicting the history of the kingdom. In 1897, British troops attacked and looted thousands of artworks, bringing them back to European museums. Recently, some museums in Germany and England have begun to return them. Note that the Kingdom of Benin is different from the present-day Republic of Benin.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The powerful Ashanti Empire in West Africa is located in which modern-day country?
giai_thich: The Ashanti Empire (Asante) was established around 1701 with its capital at Kumasi, becoming wealthy through gold and trade. The Ashanti fought the British several times in the 19th century and were annexed into the Gold Coast colony in 1902. Today, the Ashanti king (Asantehene) still holds an important traditional role in Ghana.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the most sacred symbol of the Ashanti people, believed to contain the soul of the nation?
giai_thich: According to legend, the golden stool fell from the sky into the hands of the founder of the empire, King Osei Tutu, around 1701. No one, including the king, is allowed to sit on the stool, and it must never touch the ground. In 1900, when the British governor demanded to sit on it, the Ashanti revolted in the "War of the Golden Stool."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which king of the Kingdom of Kongo converted to Christianity and actively spread the faith in the early 16th century?
giai_thich: Afonso I (Nzinga Mbemba) ruled from around 1509 to 1542, learned to read and write Portuguese, and converted to Christianity. He sent his son to Lisbon for education, and this son became one of the first black African bishops. He wrote to the King of Portugal complaining about the slave trade ravaging his kingdom.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which country colonized Madagascar?
giai_thich: France occupied Madagascar from 1895 to 1896 and overthrew the Merina dynasty, exiling the last queen, Ranavalona III, to Algeria. The Malagasy revolted in 1947 but were brutally suppressed. Madagascar gained independence in 1960. Notably, the ancestors of the Malagasy came from Indonesia and East Africa, so the Malagasy language is closely related to languages in Borneo.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which two countries did Morocco gain independence from in 1956?
giai_thich: Since 1912, most of Morocco was a French protectorate, while a strip of land in the north and south was under Spanish control. King Mohammed V, who supported the independence movement, was exiled to Madagascar by the French in 1953 but was returned in 1955. Morocco gained independence in 1956. Spain still retains the cities of Ceuta and Melilla on the Moroccan coast to this day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which country colonized Libya?
giai_thich: Italy occupied Libya from the Ottoman Empire in 1911. Leader Omar Mukhtar led a guerrilla resistance for nearly 20 years until he was captured and executed in 1931 at the age of 73. After World War II, Libya gained independence in 1951, being the first country to achieve independence through the United Nations. The name "Libya" was originally how the ancient Greeks referred to the North African region.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which country did Namibia gain independence from in 1990?
giai_thich: Namibia was formerly a German South West Africa colony. After World War I, South Africa was mandated to administer it and imposed apartheid here. The SWAPO organization fought armed struggle for many years, and Namibia gained independence on March 21, 1990, being one of the last colonies in Africa. Therefore, Germany is an option that can easily cause confusion.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the name of the first major battle of the Muslim community in 624, when about 300 people defeated an army from Mecca that was three times their size?
giai_thich: The Battle of Badr took place during Ramadan in 624, when Muhammad led about 313 people to intercept a caravan from Mecca. They defeated about 1,000 Meccan troops. The victory helped the Muslims believe that they were aided by God. The following year, in the Battle of Uhud, the Muslims were defeated.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Battle of Yarmouk in 636, which empire did the Arab Muslim forces defeat?
giai_thich: The Battle of Yarmouk took place over 6 days by the Yarmouk River (the modern-day Syria-Jordan border), led by General Khalid ibn al-Walid. The Byzantine forces were larger but were routed. After this battle, the Byzantines permanently lost Syria, Palestine, and later Egypt. Emperor Heraclius is said to have remarked 'Farewell Syria' as he departed.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Battle of Qadisiyyah in 636 paved the way for the Arabs to conquer which empire?
giai_thich: At Qadisiyyah (modern-day Iraq), the Arab forces defeated the Persian army, which included war elephants. They then captured the capital Ctesiphon with its vast treasures. By 651, the Sassanid Empire had completely collapsed. The Persians gradually converted to Islam but retained their language, unlike Egypt and Syria where Arabic replaced the old languages.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which second caliph rapidly expanded the Islamic empire and captured Jerusalem in 637-638?
giai_thich: Umar ibn al-Khattab ruled for 10 years (634-644), during which Islamic forces conquered Syria, Iraq, Egypt, and most of Persia. He was known for his simple lifestyle, wearing patched clothing. Upon entering Jerusalem, he allowed Christians to worship freely. He also established the Islamic calendar starting from the year of Hijra.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Under which caliph was the Qur'an standardized into a single version and sent to the provinces?
giai_thich: During Abu Bakr's time, parts of the Qur'an were compiled for the first time. By Uthman's time (ruling 644-656), as the empire expanded and people read the Qur'an in various ways, he ordered a standardized version to be copied and sent to major cities, commanding the destruction of other versions. The Qur'an used today is essentially based on this version.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Battle of Karbala in 680, which grandson of Muhammad was killed, an event of great significance for Shia Muslims?
giai_thich: Husayn was the son of Ali and Fatimah. He refused to submit to the Umayyad caliph Yazid and, along with about 72 family members and followers, was besieged by a large army in Karbala (Iraq). They were cut off from water and killed. Shia Muslims commemorate this event annually on Ashura. Karbala is now a sacred pilgrimage city.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What city was the capital of the Umayyad emirate and later kingdom in the Iberian Peninsula (al-Andalus)?
giai_thich: In the 10th century, Córdoba was possibly the largest city in Europe, with street lighting, public baths, and a library said to contain around 400,000 books. The Great Mosque Mezquita, with its hundreds of columns and red-and-white striped arches, is a symbol of the city. Granada was the last Islamic kingdom, existing later.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Where did Abd al-Rahman I, the only Umayyad survivor of the massacre in 750, establish an emirate?
giai_thich: When the Abbasids overthrew and massacred the Umayyads, the young prince Abd al-Rahman escaped, at one point swimming across the Euphrates River. He wandered for about 5 years through North Africa, then moved to Spain and established the emirate of Córdoba in 756. He was known as 'the Falcon of Quraysh'. The Umayyad dynasty in Spain lasted nearly 300 more years.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which dynasty founded the city of Cairo in 969?
giai_thich: The Fatimid dynasty, following the Shia line, originated from Tunisia, conquered Egypt, and built a new city named al-Qahira ('The Victorious'), which is now known as Cairo. They also established the Al-Azhar mosque and school in 970. Today, Cairo is the largest city in the Arab world, and Egyptians refer to it as 'Mother of the World'.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Caliph Harun al-Rashid, a character featured in many tales of 'One Thousand and One Nights', belonged to which dynasty?
giai_thich: Harun al-Rashid ruled from 786 to 809, during Baghdad's wealthiest and most glorious period. He had diplomatic relations with Charlemagne and is said to have gifted him an elephant named Abul-Abbas, along with an intricate water clock that amazed the Franks. In the stories, he often disguised himself as a commoner to stroll around the city at night.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The scholar Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), who lived around 965 – 1040, is most famous for his studies in which field?
giai_thich: Ibn al-Haytham demonstrated that we see objects because light from them enters the eye, rather than the eye emitting rays of light as the Greeks believed. He used experiments to test hypotheses, thus is considered one of the founders of the scientific method. He studied the camera obscura, a precursor to the camera. He wrote 'Book of Optics' while under house arrest in Cairo.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam is famous for which collection of poetry?
giai_thich: Rubaiyat consists of quatrains reflecting on the brevity of life, wine, and present joy. In 1859, Edward FitzGerald's English translation made Omar Khayyam famous worldwide. He was also a mathematician who solved cubic equations and an astronomer, contributing to the creation of the Jalali calendar, which is more accurate than the Gregorian calendar we use today.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The epic Shahnameh ("Book of Kings"), the national epic of the Iranians, was composed by whom?
giai_thich: Ferdowsi spent about 30 years writing the Shahnameh, which consists of approximately 50,000 couplets, narrating the history and legends of Persia from the creation of the world until the Arab conquest. He intentionally used very few Arabic words to preserve the Persian language. Iranians believe that thanks to Ferdowsi, the Persian language has survived to this day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Sufi poet Rumi is associated with which famous dance of the Mevlevi order?
giai_thich: Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207 – 1273) was born in what is now Afghanistan and lived in Konya (Turkey). His poetry about love and connection with God has been translated into many languages, and he is one of the most read poets in America. His students founded the Mevlevi order, where the dervishes wear white skirts and whirl as a form of meditation.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, which army did the Seljuk Turks defeat and capture their emperor?
giai_thich: Sultan Alp Arslan of the Seljuks defeated the Byzantine army at Manzikert (eastern Turkey) and captured Emperor Romanos IV. After this battle, the Turks flooded into Anatolia, marking the beginning of the region becoming "Turkey." The Byzantines weakened and sought help from the West, leading to the First Crusade.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Nizari Ismaili sect, which Europeans called "Assassins," established their main base in which fortress in Iran?
giai_thich: Hassan-i Sabbah captured the Alamut fortress in 1090. His group became famous for assassinating important figures of their enemies. The term "assassin" in English is believed to have originated from their name. In 1256, the Mongol forces of Hülegü captured and destroyed Alamut along with its famous library.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the name of the most famous and well-preserved Crusader castle located in Syria?
giai_thich: Krak des Chevaliers ("Castle of the Knights") was expanded by the Knights Hospitaller in the 12th – 13th centuries, featuring two thick walls and capable of housing about 2,000 people. Writer T. E. Lawrence called it "the most beautiful castle in the world." In 1271, Mamluk Sultan Baybars captured the castle using a forged letter ordering surrender.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Originally, the term "Mamluk" referred to whom?
giai_thich: "Mamluk" means "owned person." Young boys, primarily Turks from the steppes and Circassians from the Caucasus, were bought, converted, and trained as elite cavalry. In 1250, they overthrew their Ayyubid masters and established a dynasty that ruled Egypt and Syria for over 250 years. This is a unique case where former slaves became kings.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Mamluk general became famous at the Battle of Ain Jalut, later becoming sultan and capturing many strongholds of the Crusaders?
giai_thich: Baybars was once sold into slavery and is said to have had a cloudy eye. He commanded the vanguard at Ain Jalut in 1260. Shortly thereafter, he killed Sultan Qutuz and took the throne for himself. During his 17-year reign, he captured numerous Crusader strongholds such as Antioch and Krak des Chevaliers. He also established a postal system using horses and carrier pigeons.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did the city of Acre, the last major stronghold of the Crusaders in the Holy Land, fall?
giai_thich: In 1291, Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil besieged Acre with a large force and many catapults. After about 6 weeks, the city was captured. The remaining strongholds of the Crusaders fell or were abandoned within a few months, ending nearly 200 years of Crusader presence in the Levant. The year 1099 was when the Crusaders captured Jerusalem.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did Shah Ismail I establish the Safavid dynasty in Persia?
giai_thich: Ismail was orphaned at a young age and was the leader of a Sufi order. In 1501, at about 14 years old, he captured Tabriz and proclaimed himself Shah. He was also a poet who wrote in Turkish. The Safavid dynasty unified Iran into a nation with borders similar to those of today and lasted until 1736.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514, which empire did the Ottoman Empire defeat thanks to its superiority in guns and artillery?
giai_thich: The Ottoman army of Selim I used cannons and muskets, while the Safavid cavalry considered the use of guns cowardly. Shah Ismail was defeated and wounded. After this battle, he never fought again. The border between modern Turkey and Iran is similar to the boundary formed after these wars.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Topkapi Palace, home to the Ottoman sultans for about 400 years, is located in which city?
giai_thich: Topkapi was built in 1459 on the orders of Mehmed II, shortly after the conquest of Constantinople, on a promontory overlooking the Bosphorus Strait. It was like a small city with about 4,000 people living in the palace. Today, the palace is a museum, showcasing the Spoonmaker's Diamond and the Topkapi Dagger encrusted with emeralds.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who is the greatest architect of the Ottoman Empire, who built the Süleymaniye Mosque?
giai_thich: Mimar Sinan ("Sinan the Architect") was originally a Christian boy recruited into the Janissary corps, serving as a military engineer before becoming the royal architect. For about 50 years, he designed over 300 structures, including mosques, bridges, baths, and schools. He lived to nearly 100 years old and was buried in a small tomb next to the Süleymaniye Mosque.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which century was the Ottoman Empire referred to as the "Sick Man of Europe"?
giai_thich: This phrase is attributed to Tsar Nicholas I of Russia in the 1850s, when the empire was weakening, in debt, and losing territory. Greece, Serbia, Bulgaria, and Romania gained independence in succession. European powers competed for influence in Ottoman lands, referred to as the "Eastern Question." The empire officially ended in 1922.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What was the main demand of the "Young Turks" movement during the revolution of 1908?
giai_thich: Sultan Abdul Hamid II suspended the constitution in 1878 and ruled autocratically for 30 years. In 1908, young officers in the "Committee of Union and Progress" revolted and forced the sultan to restore the constitution. In 1909, he was deposed. Subsequently, three leaders of the movement took power and led the empire into World War I on the side of Germany.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1882, which country in North Africa did Britain occupy?
giai_thich: After Colonel Ahmed Urabi's uprising against foreign influence, Britain sent troops into Egypt to protect the Suez Canal and its debts. Egypt was nominally still part of the Ottoman Empire, but in reality, it was under British control. By 1914, Egypt officially became a British protectorate. Algeria and Tunisia were under French control, while Libya later came under Italian rule.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In the Battle of Omdurman in 1898, which force did the British, led by General Kitchener, defeat in Sudan?
giai_thich: The Mahdist state was established by Muhammad Ahmad (self-proclaimed Mahdi, "the guided one") after driving British-Egyptian forces out of Sudan in 1885. At Omdurman, the British Maxim machine guns killed about 10,000 Sudanese warriors, while the British lost only a few dozen men. A young Winston Churchill participated in this battle as a cavalry officer and reporter.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: British General Charles Gordon was killed in 1885 in which city while besieged by Mahdist forces?
giai_thich: Gordon was sent to Khartoum to evacuate Egyptians, but he decided to stay and defend the city. After nearly 10 months of siege, the city fell, and Gordon was killed just two days before the British relief force arrived. British public opinion regarded him as a martyr hero and blamed the government for the delay. Khartoum is now the capital of Sudan.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: According to contemporary records, Mansa Musa's journey through Egypt in 1324 caused the price of gold to drop for many years in which city?
giai_thich: When Mansa Musa's caravan stopped in Cairo for about three months, he spent and generously gifted gold to the extent that the amount of gold in the city surged. Historian al-Umari, who arrived in Cairo about 12 years later, noted that the price of gold had not yet recovered. This is an ancient example of how an oversupply of a commodity can decrease its value (inflation).

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Askia Muhammad was the famous emperor of which empire in West Africa?
giai_thich: Askia Muhammad (reigned 1493 – 1528) was a usurper general who later reorganized the empire with a system of bureaucracy, taxation, and standardized measurements. He encouraged Islamic scholarship, helping Timbuktu become a major academic center. His pyramid-shaped mud-brick tomb in Gao is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1591, the Songhai Empire collapsed after the Battle of Tondibi when attacked by the army of which country using firearms?
giai_thich: The Moroccan king Ahmad al-Mansur wanted to seize the gold mines in West Africa. He sent about 4,000 troops, many of whom were Spanish mercenaries, across the Sahara Desert for nearly 2,000 km. At Tondibi, firearms and cannons defeated the much larger Songhai army, which only had spears and bows. The Songhai Empire disintegrated after this battle.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Kanem-Bornu Empire in Central Africa developed around which lake?
giai_thich: Kanem-Bornu existed for about 1,000 years (from the 9th century to the 19th century) and was one of the oldest empires in Africa. The empire controlled trade routes across the Sahara connecting to Libya and Egypt. Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s due to climate change and water extraction for irrigation.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
