cau_hoi: The Swahili language in East Africa was formed from Bantu languages mixed with many words from which language?
giai_thich: Coastal port cities in East Africa like Kilwa, Mombasa, and Zanzibar traded with Arab merchants across the Indian Ocean for thousands of years. The name "Swahili" itself comes from the Arabic word "sawahil," meaning "coast." Today, Swahili has about 100 million speakers. The word "safari" (journey) in English is also a Swahili word.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1868, Ethiopian Emperor Tewodros II committed suicide when British forces attacked which fortress?
giai_thich: Tewodros II held several British missionaries and diplomats hostage because he was angry that Queen Victoria did not respond to his letters. Britain sent about 13,000 troops from India to rescue them. When the British captured the fortress of Magdala, Tewodros used the very pistol that Queen Victoria had given him to commit suicide. The British then withdrew, taking many treasures with them.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which city in Ethiopia was once the capital in the 17th century, famous for its stone castles likened to the "Camelot of Africa"?
giai_thich: Emperor Fasilides established Gondar as the capital around 1636. Subsequent emperors built many castles, churches, and baths in the royal enclosure, with architecture blending Ethiopian, Indian, and Portuguese styles. Gondar was the capital of Ethiopia for about 200 years. The Fasil Ghebbi complex is now a World Heritage site.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What does the name of Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, established in 1886, mean?
giai_thich: Empress Taytu, wife of Emperor Menelik II, loved the hot springs in the area and chose this place to build a house, naming it Addis Ababa ("New Flower"). To provide firewood for the city, many eucalyptus trees imported from Australia were planted. Addis Ababa is located at an altitude of about 2,350 meters, making it one of the highest capitals in the world.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which country in southern Africa was founded by King Moshoeshoe I?
giai_thich: In the early 19th century, during a time of chaotic wars in southern Africa, Moshoeshoe gathered refugees on Thaba Bosiu mountain, a natural fortress that was hard to attack. He skillfully negotiated and sought British protection to avoid being taken over by the Boer settlers. Lesotho is completely surrounded by South Africa, and the entire country is at an altitude of over 1,000 meters.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The "Great Trek" in the 1830s in South Africa was the migration of which group of people?
giai_thich: About 12,000 to 15,000 dissatisfied Boer people with British rule in the Cape Colony, especially after the abolition of slavery, moved inland with ox wagons and established their own republics like Transvaal and Orange Free State. Along the way, they clashed with African tribes, including the Zulu.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The "Big Hole" diamond mine, one of the largest hand-dug holes in the world, is located in which city in South Africa?
giai_thich: After diamonds were discovered in 1871, tens of thousands of people flocked to dig with shovels, creating a hole about 240 meters deep. For over 40 years, the mine produced about 2,700 kg of diamonds. Cecil Rhodes made his fortune here and founded the De Beers company. The city of Kimberley was the first in the Southern Hemisphere to have electric streetlights.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The city of Johannesburg in South Africa was founded in 1886 due to the discovery of which resource?
giai_thich: In 1886, a large gold vein was discovered in the Witwatersrand region. In just 10 years, a mining camp turned into a populous city, and Johannesburg was called "Egoli," meaning "Place of Gold." Witwatersrand is the largest gold mine in the world, providing about 40% of the gold ever mined in history. The British's desire to control the gold led to the Boer War.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When was the African National Congress (ANC), Nelson Mandela's party, founded?
giai_thich: The ANC was founded in 1912 (initially named the South African Native National Congress), just two years after the Union of South Africa was established, to fight for the rights of black people. It is one of the oldest liberation movements in Africa. The ANC was banned from 1960 to 1990, and since 1994, it has been the ruling party in South Africa.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did the National Party come to power and begin to officially impose apartheid in South Africa?
giai_thich: In 1948, the Afrikaner National Party won the election with the slogan "apartheid." They enacted a series of laws: classifying people by race, banning interracial marriage, and segregating living areas. Black people were relegated to impoverished "homelands." This regime lasted for 46 years, until 1994.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Steve Biko, the South African activist who died while in police custody in 1977, led which movement?
giai_thich: Steve Biko was a medical student. His movement encouraged black people to take pride in themselves and reject the inferiority complex imposed by apartheid. He was beaten by police while in custody and died at the age of 30. His death sparked outrage worldwide, and singer Peter Gabriel wrote the song "Biko" in his memory.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Léopold Sédar Senghor, the poet who initiated the Négritude movement, was the first president of which country?
giai_thich: Senghor studied in Paris and was the first African elected to the French Academy. The Négritude movement, initiated by him and other poets, aimed to affirm the cultural value of black people. He served as president of Senegal for 20 years (1960 – 1980) and was one of the first African presidents to voluntarily step down from office.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1958, which West African country led by Ahmed Sékou Touré voted "no" to France's proposal and gained immediate independence?
giai_thich: French President de Gaulle proposed that colonies remain in a "French Community." Only Guinea voted against it. Sékou Touré declared: "We prefer to be poor in freedom than rich in slavery." France immediately withdrew, taking away machinery, records, and even removing light bulbs. Other French colonies gained independence in 1960.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1984, what did Thomas Sankara rename Upper Volta to?
giai_thich: Burkina Faso means "Land of Honest People," derived from two local languages. Sankara came to power in 1983 at the age of 33. He sold the government's fleet of Mercedes cars, drove a cheap Renault 5, planted millions of trees, and vaccinated about 2.5 million children. He was assassinated in a coup in 1987.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1975, what was the name of the country Dahomey in West Africa changed to?
giai_thich: Dahomey was the name of a powerful kingdom in history, famous for its female warriors known to Europeans as the "Dahomey Amazons." In 1975, the government changed the country's name to Benin, after the Benin Gulf, to avoid favoring the Fon ethnicity of the former Dahomey kingdom. It should not be confused with the historical Kingdom of Benin, located in present-day Nigeria.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Why is 1960 referred to as "The Year of Africa"?
giai_thich: In 1960, 17 countries gained independence, including 14 former French colonies, Nigeria, Somalia, and Belgian Congo. This changed the balance in the United Nations, where the newly independent countries became an important force. That same year, British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan spoke of "the winds of change blowing across this continent."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What is the abbreviation for the front that led the war for Algeria's independence (1954 – 1962)?
giai_thich: The FLN (National Liberation Front) began the war with a series of attacks on November 1, 1954. After Algeria gained independence in 1962, the FLN became the only ruling party for many years. The film "The Battle of Algiers" (1966) tells the story of this struggle and is still studied today. ANC is from South Africa, MPLA is from Angola, and SWAPO is from Namibia.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which country did the MPLA movement fight for independence?
giai_thich: The MPLA (People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola) was led by poet-doctor Agostinho Neto. Angola gained independence in 1975, but three liberation movements (MPLA, UNITA, FNLA) turned against each other, and Cold War powers intervened. The MPLA gained control of the capital Luanda and has been in power ever since.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which national liberation struggle did the FRELIMO front lead against Portugal?
giai_thich: FRELIMO was founded in 1962 and began armed struggle in 1964. Mozambique gained independence on June 25, 1975, with Samora Machel as its first president. The country then fell into a civil war that lasted until 1992. The flag of Mozambique is one of the few national flags that features an AK-47 rifle.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Amílcar Cabral was a leader of the liberation movement for which countries?
giai_thich: Amílcar Cabral was an agricultural engineer who founded the PAIGC party in 1956. His movement controlled much of Guinea-Bissau and was praised for building schools and health stations in liberated areas. He was assassinated in 1973, just months before Guinea-Bissau declared independence. He is regarded as one of Africa's great thinkers.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What was the consequence of the "Carnation Revolution" in Portugal in 1974?
D: The King of Portugal returned to the throne
giai_thich: On April 25, 1974, military officers tired of prolonged colonial wars overthrew the dictatorship in Lisbon with little bloodshed. People placed carnations in the barrels of soldiers' guns. The new government quickly granted independence to Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cabo Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Angola in 1974-1975.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Kwame Nkrumah was a strong advocate of which ideology?
giai_thich: Nkrumah believed that African countries could only be truly strong when united as a "United States of Africa." He stated, "Africa must unite or perish." He contributed to the establishment of the Organization of African Unity in 1963. Ujamaa is the policy of Julius Nyerere in Tanzania, while Négritude is a literary movement by Senghor.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did Mussolini's Italy invade Ethiopia?
giai_thich: In October 1935, Italy attacked Ethiopia, using aircraft and chemical weapons against both military and civilians. The League of Nations imposed weak sanctions, highlighting the organization's impotence. In 1936, Italian forces captured Addis Ababa. The year 1896 was when Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa, while 1911 was the year Italy invaded Libya.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: After the Six-Day War in 1967, when was the Suez Canal closed until?
giai_thich: The Suez Canal became a frontline between Israeli and Egyptian forces, and ships could not pass through. Fourteen ships were trapped in the canal for eight years, and their crews formed the "Great Bitter Lake Association," even organizing their own "Olympics." The canal reopened on June 5, 1975, after being cleared of mines.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did the Sassanid Empire fall completely to the Arabs?
giai_thich: After defeats at Qadisiyyah (636) and Nahavand (642), the last Sassanid king Yazdegerd III fled eastward. In 651, he was killed in Merv (present-day Turkmenistan). His son fled to China seeking help from the Tang dynasty but was unsuccessful. The Sassanid Empire lasted about 400 years and was a formidable rival to Rome.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Before the emergence of Islam, what was the main religion of the Persians?
giai_thich: Zoroastrianism was founded by the prophet Zarathustra (Zoroaster) and believes in the battle between good and evil. Fire is a sacred symbol, so temples always keep a flame burning. Today, there are only about 100,000 to 200,000 followers, mostly Parsis in India. Singer Freddie Mercury was born into a Parsi family.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which city did the Qajar dynasty (1789 – 1925) choose as the capital of Iran?
giai_thich: Aga Mohammad Khan, the founder of the Qajar dynasty, chose Tehran, which was then just a small town, as the capital in 1786 because it was close to his tribe's base in the north. Since then, Tehran has developed into the capital of Iran to this day, with over 9 million residents. Isfahan was the capital during the Safavid era, while Shiraz was the capital during the Zand dynasty.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Around which year did the Constitutional Revolution in Persia, leading to the establishment of the first parliament, occur?
giai_thich: The people of Persia, including merchants, clerics, and intellectuals, opposed the Qajar king's sale of economic privileges to foreigners. In 1906, thousands of people occupied the British embassy grounds, forcing the king to agree to establish a parliament (Majlis) and enact a constitution. This was the first constitutional revolution in the Middle East.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year was Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, who nationalized the oil industry, overthrown in a coup?
giai_thich: In 1951, Mosaddegh nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (the predecessor of BP). In 1953, the CIA and British intelligence supported a coup to overthrow him, restoring the Shah to power. In 2013, the CIA officially acknowledged its role. This event contributed to Iranian distrust of the West and is a deep-rooted cause of the 1979 revolution.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did Reza Khan ascend to the throne, establishing the Pahlavi dynasty in Iran?
giai_thich: Reza Khan was originally an officer in the Cossack Brigade. He staged a coup in 1921, then was recognized by parliament as king in 1925 after deposing the Qajar dynasty. He modernized the country with railways and schools but also banned women from wearing veils and ruled autocratically. In 1941, Britain and the Soviet Union forced him to abdicate due to suspicions of his ties to Germany.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: After World War I, Iraq was placed under the mandate of which country?
giai_thich: The League of Nations assigned Iraq to British administration. In 1921, Britain installed Prince Faisal, the son of Sharif Hussein of Mecca, as king of Iraq, despite him not being Iraqi. Iraq's borders combined three former Ottoman provinces (Mosul, Baghdad, Basra) with very different communities: Kurds, Sunni Arabs, and Shia Arabs. Iraq gained independence in 1932.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: After World War I, Syria and Lebanon were placed under the mandate of which country?
giai_thich: In 1920, Faisal (later king of Iraq) proclaimed himself king of Syria, but was defeated by French forces just months later. France separated Lebanon into a distinct region, with a significant Christian population. Both Syria and Lebanon gained independence between 1943 and 1946. To this day, French is still widely spoken in Lebanon.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: King Abdullah I of Jordan and the current Jordanian kings belong to which dynasty?
giai_thich: The Hashemite dynasty claims direct descent from the Prophet Muhammad. They ruled Mecca for many centuries. After World War I, two sons of Sharif Hussein became kings: Abdullah in Transjordan (Jordan) and Faisal in Iraq. The Hashemite dynasty in Iraq was overthrown in 1958, while in Jordan they continue to reign to this day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who initiated the Arab revolt against the Ottoman Empire in 1916?
giai_thich: Sharif Hussein governed Mecca under Ottoman rule. He promised to support an independent Arab kingdom if he revolted, through letters exchanged with British High Commissioner McMahon. He declared the uprising in June 1916, and his sons, especially Faisal, led the fighting. Later, Hussein was defeated by Ibn Saud and lost the Hejaz region.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The first Arab country to become a member of the League of Nations in 1932 was which country?
giai_thich: When the British mandate ended in 1932, Iraq became an independent kingdom and joined the League of Nations. However, Britain retained military bases and significant influence in Iraq under the 1930 treaty. Egypt joined the League of Nations later, in 1937.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Arab League was founded in 1945 in which city?
giai_thich: On March 22, 1945, seven countries including Egypt, Iraq, Jordan (Transjordan), Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Yemen signed the charter to establish the Arab League in Cairo. Today, the organization has 22 members across Asia and Africa. Its headquarters is in Cairo, only moving to Tunis for about 10 years (1979 – 1989) after Egypt signed a peace treaty with Israel.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did the United Nations approve the plan to partition Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state?
giai_thich: On November 29, 1947, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 181, partitioning Palestine into two states, with Jerusalem placed under international administration. The Jewish side accepted, while the Arab side opposed. Conflict erupted shortly thereafter, and in 1948 Israel declared its establishment. The Arab state as planned was never established.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Golda Meir, the first female Prime Minister of Israel, grew up in which country before emigrating to Palestine?
giai_thich: Golda Meir was born in 1898 in Kiev (Russian Empire), but her family emigrated to America when she was about 8 years old, and she grew up in Milwaukee, working as a teacher. In 1921, she moved to Palestine. She served as Prime Minister from 1969 to 1974 and was referred to as "the only man in the cabinet" due to her tough personality.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When did Israel complete the return of the entire Sinai Peninsula to Egypt?
giai_thich: According to the peace treaty in 1979, Israel withdrew its troops from Sinai in phases. On April 25, 1982, the final phase was completed, and Israel had to evacuate the settlement town of Yamit. April 25 is now Sinai Liberation Day in Egypt. The small area of Taba on the coast was returned only in 1989 after an international arbitration ruling.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year was the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) established?
giai_thich: The PLO was established at a conference in East Jerusalem in 1964, with the support of the Arab League. From 1969, Yasser Arafat led the PLO for 35 years. In 1974, the PLO was recognized by the United Nations as the representative of the Palestinian people. In 1993, the PLO and Israel recognized each other in the Oslo Accords.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When did the first Palestinian uprising in the West Bank and Gaza, known as the Intifada, begin?
giai_thich: The Intifada (meaning "to shake off") began in December 1987 after a traffic accident in Gaza killed four Palestinians. Protesters, many of whom were youths, threw stones, organized strikes, and boycotted Israeli goods. The movement lasted until around 1993 and contributed to the Oslo Accords. The second Intifada began in 2000.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In what year did Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who ruled for nearly 30 years, have to resign?
giai_thich: Mubarak became president in 1981 after Sadat was assassinated. In 2011, hundreds of thousands gathered in Tahrir Square (Cairo) for 18 days demanding his departure during the Arab Spring wave. On February 11, 2011, he resigned, and power was handed over to the military. 2013 was the year elected President Mohamed Morsi was ousted by the military.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1971, which Gulf emirates ended British protectorate status and formed a federation, now consisting of 7 emirates?
giai_thich: On December 2, 1971, six emirates including Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm al-Quwain, and Fujairah established the UAE. Ras al-Khaimah joined in early 1972. Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi became the first president. Thanks to oil, poor fishing villages and pearl divers quickly transformed into modern cities like Dubai.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: From which country did Kuwait gain independence in 1961?
giai_thich: Kuwait was a British protectorate from 1899. Immediately after Kuwait gained independence in 1961, Iraq claimed Kuwait as part of its territory, and Britain had to send troops for protection. Iraq again claimed sovereignty when it invaded Kuwait in 1990. Kuwait has about 6% of the world's oil reserves despite its very small size.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which country did Sultan Qaboos rule for nearly 50 years (1970 – 2020)?
giai_thich: In 1970, Qaboos overthrew his father, who ruled Oman in a very conservative manner. At that time, Oman had only about 10 km of paved roads and 3 schools. Qaboos used oil money to build a modern nation. He pursued a neutral foreign policy, helping Oman become a mediator between many countries. He passed away in 2020.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When did North Yemen and South Yemen unite into one country?
giai_thich: North Yemen was once a kingdom and then a republic, while South Yemen was the British colony of Aden, gaining independence in 1967 and becoming the only socialist state in the Arab world. On May 22, 1990, the two regions united to form the Republic of Yemen. In 1994, a brief civil war occurred when the south attempted to secede.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1981, which country's nuclear reactor, Osirak, did Israel bomb and destroy?
giai_thich: On June 7, 1981, Israeli fighter jets flew over Jordanian and Saudi airspace, destroying the Osirak reactor being built near Baghdad, fearing that Iraq would develop nuclear weapons. The United Nations Security Council condemned the attack. The reactor was supplied by France.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which countries first normalized diplomatic relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords in 2020?
giai_thich: In September 2020, at the White House, Israel signed agreements to establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, with the U.S. as a mediator. Later, Morocco and Sudan also joined. These were the first Arab countries to recognize Israel since Jordan in 1994. The name of the agreement is derived from Abraham, a common patriarch of Jews and Arabs according to tradition.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: What term do Palestinians use to refer to the events of 1948, when about 700,000 people were forced to leave their homes?
giai_thich: During the 1948 war, about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from villages and cities, and many were not allowed to return. Many families still keep the keys to their old homes as a symbol. Today, their descendants number in the millions of refugees living in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, and the Palestinian territories. May 15 is Nakba Memorial Day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which ethnic group, numbering around 30-40 million people, primarily living in Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria, is often referred to as the largest nation in the world without a state?
giai_thich: After World War I, the Treaty of Sèvres promised a state for the Kurds, but the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 replaced it and nullified that promise. The Kurds have their own language and culture. Today, they have an autonomous region in northern Iraq with its capital in Erbil. Sultan Saladin was also Kurdish. The Armenians have had their own state.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When did the civil war in Syria begin?
giai_thich: In 2011, during the Arab Spring, protests against the government erupted in Syria, which then escalated into a civil war with the intervention of many countries. The war has resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths and over 12 million people displaced, marking the largest refugee crisis of the 21st century. The ancient city of Aleppo was heavily devastated.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Manden Charter (Kouroukan Fouga), considered one of the first human rights charters in history, was issued around 1236 by the emperor who founded which empire?
giai_thich: After the historic victory at the Battle of Kirina in 1235, Sundiata Keita unified the tribes and established the powerful Mali Empire in West Africa. At the Kurukan Fuga assembly, he and the leaders issued a charter consisting of 44 articles on equality, social peace, and the protection of women. In 2009, UNESCO officially recognized the Manden Charter as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1652, why did the Dutch East India Company establish Cape Town at the southern tip of Africa?
B: To build a fortress against the Portuguese
C: To serve as a slave trading center
D: To act as a supply station for ships going to Asia
giai_thich: Jan van Riebeeck was sent with about 90 people to grow vegetables, raise livestock, and provide fresh water for ships on long journeys to Indonesia, helping sailors avoid scurvy due to vitamin deficiency. The original vegetable garden is now the Company's Garden in central Cape Town. The Dutch settlers are the ancestors of the Boers.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Scottish explorer is famous for his explorations of which river in West Africa?
giai_thich: At that time, Europeans did not know which direction the Niger River flowed. In 1796, Mungo Park was the first European to document that the Niger River flowed eastward. On his second trip in 1806, he drowned at the Bussa rapids while being attacked. It wasn't until 1830 that Europeans learned that the Niger River emptied into the Gulf of Guinea.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which explorer identified Lake Victoria as the main source of the White Nile?
giai_thich: In 1858, during an expedition with Richard Burton, Speke traveled alone to a large lake that he named Victoria after Queen Victoria, declaring it the source of the Nile. Burton did not believe him, and the two had a fierce argument. Speke died in a hunting accident in 1864, just before a public debate with Burton. Later, Stanley confirmed that Speke was correct.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1855, what did David Livingstone name the large waterfall on the Zambezi River?
giai_thich: The local people called the falls "Mosi-oa-Tunya," meaning "The Smoke That Thunders," due to the mist rising hundreds of meters and the sound echoing far away. Livingstone was the first European to document the falls and named them after Queen Victoria. The falls are about 1.7 km wide, making them one of the largest waterfalls in the world, located on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When did France begin its conquest of Algeria?
giai_thich: In 1827, the governor of Algiers, during an argument, struck the French consul with a fan. France used this as a pretext to attack and occupy Algiers in 1830. The conquest of all of Algeria took decades due to fierce resistance. Algeria was ruled by France for 132 years, until 1962.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the famous leader that led the Algerian resistance against the French from 1832 to 1847?
giai_thich: Emir Abd al-Qadir was a religious scholar and warrior who established a state with its own army and tax system to resist the French for 15 years. After surrendering, he lived in exile in Damascus. In 1860, he saved thousands of Christians from a riot, earning worldwide praise. A town in the U.S. (Elkader, Iowa) is named after him.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the first president of independent Algeria?
giai_thich: Ben Bella was one of the founders of the FLN and was imprisoned by the French from 1956 to 1962. He served as prime minister and then president, but in 1965 he was overthrown by his own defense minister, Houari Boumediene, and imprisoned for about 15 years. In his youth, he played football for the French club Olympique de Marseille.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Samori Touré led the resistance against French colonialism in which region of Africa?
giai_thich: Samori Touré established the Wassoulou Empire and resisted the French for about 16 years (1882 – 1898). He had his own workshop for manufacturing and repairing guns, and when pressured, he moved the entire empire eastward. In 1898 he was captured and died in exile. His nephew, Ahmed Sékou Touré, became the first president of Guinea.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Maji Maji uprising (1905 – 1907) in Tanganyika erupted against the colonial power of which country?
giai_thich: The people were forced by the German colonial government to grow cotton for export. A sorcerer distributed "magic water" (maji) and claimed it would turn bullets into water. Many different ethnic groups rose up. The Germans suppressed the uprising with a policy of burning villages and destroying crops, leading to a famine that could have caused hundreds of thousands of deaths.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The genocide of the Herero and Nama (1904 – 1908) in Namibia was carried out by the army of which country?
giai_thich: When the Herero and Nama rose up against land dispossession, German General Lothar von Trotha ordered their extermination, driving tens of thousands into the waterless Omaheke desert. About 80% of the Herero and half of the Nama died. This is considered the first genocide of the 20th century. In 2021, the German government officially recognized it as genocide.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Queen Nzinga is famous for her struggle against Portuguese colonialism in which region?
B: Angola (the kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba)
giai_thich: Nzinga (circa 1583 – 1663) was a wise and courageous queen. Legend has it that when she went to negotiate with the Portuguese governor and was not invited to sit, she signaled for a servant to kneel down to serve as a chair so she could sit at the same level. She commanded the army against the Portuguese for decades. Today, she is a national hero of Angola.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which Ashanti queen led the "War of the Golden Stool" against the British in 1900?
giai_thich: When the Ashanti king was exiled and the British governor demanded to sit on the Golden Stool, the male leaders hesitated. Yaa Asantewaa, then about 60 years old, stood up and declared that if the men would not fight, the women would take up arms. She led the siege of the British fort in Kumasi for many months. Eventually, she was captured and exiled to Seychelles, but the British never obtained the Golden Stool.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Ranavalona I was a famous queen who resisted European influence in which country in the 19th century?
giai_thich: Ranavalona I ruled Madagascar from 1828 to 1861. She expelled missionaries, banned Christianity, and ruled very strictly to protect the kingdom's independence from Britain and France. In 1845, her forces defeated a joint attack by British and French warships. Historians still debate her legacy.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The sultans who ruled Zanzibar in the 19th century originated from which country on the Arabian Peninsula?
giai_thich: Sultan Said bin Sultan of Oman moved the capital from Muscat to Zanzibar in 1840 because the island was wealthy from clove cultivation and trade. After his death, Zanzibar and Oman separated into two distinct kingdoms. The Omani sultans ruled Zanzibar until the revolution in 1964. Today, Zanzibar still has many beautifully carved wooden doors in the Arab style.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Buganda Kingdom, a powerful traditional kingdom in East Africa, is located in which modern-day country?
giai_thich: Buganda is located on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, and the name Uganda is derived from this kingdom's name. When Stanley arrived in 1875, he was amazed at how well-organized the court was. The king of Buganda is called "Kabaka." Today, Buganda still exists as a traditional kingdom within Uganda, and the capital, Kampala, is located within its territory.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Ogaden War (1977 – 1978) occurred between Ethiopia and which country?
giai_thich: Somalia sought to annex the Ogaden region of Ethiopia, where many Somali people lived. Initially, Somali forces advanced quickly, but the Soviet Union shifted its support to Ethiopia, and Cuba sent tens of thousands of troops, helping Ethiopia to win. This is an example of how the Cold War influenced conflicts in Africa.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Kenneth Kaunda was the first president of which country, ruling for 27 years?
giai_thich: Kaunda led Northern Rhodesia to independence in 1964, renaming it Zambia. He supported liberation movements in Zimbabwe, Namibia, and South Africa. He was known for the white handkerchief he always carried. In 1991, he lost in the first multi-party elections and accepted a peaceful exit from office. He lived to the age of 97.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Seretse Khama was the first president of which country in southern Africa?
giai_thich: Seretse Khama was a descendant of tribal leaders. When he married a white British woman in 1948, the British government, under pressure from apartheid South Africa, exiled him from his homeland for many years. He returned and led Botswana to independence in 1966. Botswana later became one of the most democratic and stable countries in Africa due to its good management of diamond resources.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Hastings Banda, who ruled for a long time and self-proclaimed as "life president," led which country?
giai_thich: Hastings Banda worked as a doctor in the US and UK for many years. He returned to lead the independence movement, and Nyasaland became Malawi in 1964. He ruled autocratically for about 30 years, imposing strict regulations such as banning women from wearing trousers. In 1994, he lost in the first multi-party elections.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, the first elected female president in Africa, led which country?
giai_thich: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf studied economics at Harvard University, worked for the World Bank, and was imprisoned for opposing the military regime. She was elected president in 2005 after a brutal civil war in Liberia, taking office in early 2006. In 2011, she shared the Nobel Peace Prize with two other women for fighting for women's rights.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Wangari Maathai, the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize (2004), is famous for which movement?
giai_thich: Wangari Maathai was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate. In 1977, she founded the Green Belt Movement in Kenya, helping rural women plant over 50 million trees to combat soil erosion and generate income. She was arrested and beaten multiple times for protesting land grabs. She passed away in 2011.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the first African Secretary-General of the United Nations, was from which country?
giai_thich: Boutros-Ghali was an international law professor and a Coptic Christian diplomat from Egypt. He played a significant role in the Egypt-Israel peace treaty. He served as Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1992 to 1996, during a period marked by crises in Somalia, Rwanda, and Bosnia. He is the only Secretary-General to serve a single term due to US opposition to his re-election.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The writer Chinua Achebe, author of the famous novel "Things Fall Apart," was from which country?
giai_thich: "Things Fall Apart" (1958) tells the story of Okonkwo, an Igbo warrior, and the disintegration of traditional society as Europeans arrive. The book has sold over 20 million copies and has been translated into about 50 languages, making it the most widely read African novel in the world. Achebe is referred to as the "father of modern African literature."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Wole Soyinka, the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, is a citizen of which country?
giai_thich: Wole Soyinka is a playwright and poet from the Yoruba ethnic group. He was imprisoned for nearly two years, mostly in solitary confinement, during the Nigerian Civil War for calling for a ceasefire. In prison, he wrote on toilet paper and between the lines of books. After him, other African writers like Naguib Mahfouz (Egypt, 1988) and Nadine Gordimer (South Africa, 1991) also won the prize.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The legendary female warrior Amina was the queen of the city-state of Zazzau, belonging to which ethnic group in northern Nigeria today?
giai_thich: Amina lived around the 16th century and is said to have commanded about 20,000 troops, expanding her territory and forcing other city-states to pay tribute. She is believed to have built earthen walls around cities, known as "ganuwar Amina." The city-state of Zazzau is now the city of Zaria. Today, there is a statue of her riding a horse, holding a spear, as a symbol of Nigerian women's strength in Lagos.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Fashoda crisis in 1898 in Sudan nearly caused a war between Britain and which country?
giai_thich: France wanted a colonial strip from west to east Africa, while Britain wanted a strip from north to south. A small French force arrived in Fashoda on the Nile and encountered a larger army led by General Kitchener. After weeks of tension, France withdrew. The two countries later resolved their differences and became allies in the "Entente Cordiale" in 1904.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The idea of building the railway "From Cape to Cairo" across Africa was the plan of which empire?
giai_thich: Cecil Rhodes dreamed of a continuous British colony from Cape Town to Cairo, connected by railway. The plan was hindered by German East Africa lying in between, until after World War I. The railway was never completed, but many sections were built and still exist today. This symbolizes the ambitions of British imperialism.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Agadir Crisis of 1911 in Morocco, when a warship was sent to Agadir port, was a confrontation between France and which country?
giai_thich: When France sent troops into the city of Fez, Germany dispatched the gunboat Panther to Agadir port to protest and demand compensation. Britain sided with France. Ultimately, Germany accepted French control over Morocco in exchange for a portion of territory in French Congo. The crisis further strained relations among European powers, contributing to World War I.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Scholar Ibn Khaldun, author of the "Muqaddimah" and considered one of the founders of sociology, was born in which city?
giai_thich: Ibn Khaldun (1332 – 1406) was born in Tunis to a family of al-Andalus origin. In the "Muqaddimah" (Introduction), he explains the rise and fall of dynasties through the concept of "asabiyyah" (group solidarity), and analyzes economic and social issues scientifically. In 1401, he even met Timur when this conqueror besieged Damascus.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The geographer al-Idrisi created the famous world map in 1154 for which king?
giai_thich: Al-Idrisi was a Muslim scholar working at the court of the Norman King Roger II in Palermo (Sicily). He spent about 15 years gathering information from merchants and sailors to create the most detailed world map of his time. Interestingly, the map had south at the top, following the tradition of Islamic cartographers.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, one of the oldest surviving Islamic structures, was built during the reign of which caliph?
giai_thich: Caliph Abd al-Malik of the Umayyad dynasty commissioned the Dome of the Rock, completed around 691, on the Temple Mount, which is also sacred to Jews. The dome is now covered in gold (renovated in 1993). According to Islamic tradition, this is where Muhammad ascended to heaven during the "Night Journey." Saladin recaptured Jerusalem nearly 500 years later.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year was the city of Córdoba recaptured by Christian kingdoms during the Reconquista?
giai_thich: King Ferdinand III of Castile captured Córdoba in 1236, and the great mosque Mezquita was converted into a church. In the 16th century, a large church was built right in the middle of the mosque. Emperor Charles V lamented that they had destroyed "a unique thing in the world" to build something that could be seen anywhere.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 929, who declared the establishment of the caliphate kingdom of Córdoba, self-proclaiming as caliph in al-Andalus?
giai_thich: Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed himself caliph to assert equality with the Abbasid dynasty in Baghdad and the Fatimid dynasty in North Africa. Under his rule (912 – 961), Córdoba reached its peak in wealth and culture. He commissioned the magnificent palace city of Medina Azahara near Córdoba. Legend has it that he said he had only 14 truly happy days in his life.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Almoravid dynasty, which once ruled Morocco and Spain, originated from which region?
giai_thich: The Almoravids originated from the nomadic Berber tribes of the Sanhaja in the Sahara Desert, with men in the tribe covering their faces with scarves. They followed a strict Islamic preacher and conquered Morocco, then moved to Spain to defeat the Castilian forces in 1086. Their gold coin, the dinar, became so popular that Europeans also used it.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which dynasty founded the city of Marrakesh in Morocco around 1070?
giai_thich: The Almoravid dynasty established Marrakesh as its capital. The city is famous for its red walls, hence called the "Red City," and the bustling Jemaa el-Fnaa square filled with storytellers, snake charmers, and food stalls. The name Morocco in many European languages derives from the name Marrakesh.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Alaouite dynasty, which still rules Morocco today, began its reign in which century?
giai_thich: The Alaouite dynasty has been in power since around 1631 – 1666, making it one of the oldest ruling dynasties in the world. They claim descent from the prophet Muhammad. King Moulay Ismail (reigned 1672 – 1727) is famous for building the capital Meknes with stables for about 12,000 horses. The current king of Morocco is Mohammed VI.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1798, Napoleon defeated the Mamluk cavalry near Cairo in a battle known as what?
giai_thich: Before the battle, Napoleon is said to have told his soldiers: "Forty centuries are looking down upon you from the summit of these pyramids." The French troops formed square formations against the charges of the Mamluk cavalry. In fact, the battle took place about 15 km from the pyramids. The Battle of Abukir Bay was the naval battle in which the French were defeated by Nelson.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1811, Muhammad Ali Pasha eliminated the leaders of which group during the massacre at the Citadel of Cairo?
giai_thich: Muhammad Ali invited the Mamluk leaders to a ceremony at the Citadel of Cairo, then closed the gates and shot them down in the narrow passage. According to legend, only one survived by jumping his horse over the city wall. This event ended the power of the Mamluks in Egypt after about 550 years and allowed Muhammad Ali to seize full control.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1826, Sultan Mahmud II dissolved which force in an event referred to by the Turks as the "Blessed Event"?
giai_thich: The Janissary Corps was once an elite force but gradually became conservative, revolting multiple times and overthrowing sultans to resist reforms. In 1826, when they revolted again, Mahmud II used new artillery to fire on their barracks, killing thousands and dissolving the force. He then built a modern army in the European style.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When did the Tanzimat reform period ("reorganization") in the Ottoman Empire begin?
giai_thich: In 1839, the Gülhane Edict promised to protect the lives, property, and equal rights of all subjects, regardless of their religion. During the Tanzimat period (1839 – 1876), the empire established new schools, a postal system, telegraph, and new laws modeled after Europe. The reforms aimed to prevent the multi-ethnic empire from disintegrating.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: When was the first constitution of the Ottoman Empire promulgated?
giai_thich: In 1876, under pressure from reformers known as the "Young Ottomans," Sultan Abdul Hamid II issued a constitution and convened the first parliament. However, just about two years later, under the pretext of war with Russia, he dissolved the parliament and suspended the constitution for 30 years. The constitution was only restored after the Young Turk Revolution in 1908.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Hejaz railway, built in the early 20th century to transport pilgrims, connected Damascus to which city?
giai_thich: The railway was inaugurated in 1908, shortening the journey to the holy site from about 40 days by camel to around 5 days. The plan to extend to Mecca was never completed. During World War I, the line was sabotaged multiple times by Lawrence of Arabia and Arab forces. Today, old abandoned train cars can still be seen in the desert.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Which British archaeologist and explorer, known as the "Queen of the Desert," established the Iraq Museum?
giai_thich: Gertrude Bell was one of the first women to graduate with honors in history from Oxford. She traveled throughout the Arabian desert, spoke Arabic and Persian, and became a British intelligence officer. She contributed to delineating borders and bringing Faisal to the throne of Iraq. In 1926, she established the Iraq Museum in Baghdad and passed away that same year.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who chaired the Cairo Conference in 1921, where the British decided to install Faisal as king of Iraq and Abdullah to govern Transjordan?
giai_thich: In 1921, Winston Churchill served as Colonial Secretary and convened about 40 Middle Eastern experts in Cairo, including Gertrude Bell and T. E. Lawrence. The conference largely determined the political map of the Middle East in favor of Britain and at a lower military cost. The attendees jokingly referred to themselves as the "Forty Thieves."

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The revolution on July 14, 1958, overthrew the monarchy in which country?
giai_thich: Military officers led by Abd al-Karim Qasim seized Baghdad, killing King Faisal II, who was only 23 years old at the time, along with many royal family members. Iraq became a republic. The revolution ended the Hashemite monarchy in Iraq, while Faisal II's cousin, King Hussein, continued to reign in Jordan.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year was King Idris of Libya overthrown by Muammar Gaddafi in a coup?
giai_thich: Idris I was the first and only king of independent Libya (since 1951). While he was receiving medical treatment in Turkey in 1969, a group of young officers led by Gaddafi staged a coup with almost no bloodshed. Idris lived in exile in Egypt until his death in 1983 at the age of 94. The flag from his reign was reused by the rebels in 2011.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Ba'ath Party, which once ruled both Syria and Iraq, was founded in which city?
giai_thich: The Ba'ath Party ("Renaissance") was founded in Damascus in 1947 by two Syrian intellectuals, Michel Aflaq (a Christian) and Salah al-Din al-Bitar (a Sunni Muslim). The party advocated for the unity of Arab peoples, socialism, and a secular state. Later, the two branches of Ba'ath in Syria and Iraq became rivals.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did Hafez al-Assad take power in Syria?
giai_thich: Hafez al-Assad, a pilot and defense minister, seized power through a coup he called the "Correction Movement" in 1970. He ruled Syria for 30 years until his death in 2000. His son, Bashar al-Assad, an ophthalmologist who studied in London, succeeded him and has been in power until the end of 2024. 1963 was the year the Ba'ath Party took control in Syria.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Taif Agreement of 1989, signed in Saudi Arabia, ended the civil war in which country?
giai_thich: Lebanese lawmakers met in the city of Taif and agreed to share power equally between Christians and Muslims in parliament, instead of the previous 6:5 ratio favoring Christians. The agreement ended the 15-year civil war in 1990. Traditionally, the president of Lebanon is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister is Sunni, and the speaker of parliament is Shia.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The 1991 Middle East Peace Conference, where Israel first negotiated directly with Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and the Palestinians, was held in which city?
giai_thich: After the Gulf War, the US and the Soviet Union jointly organized the Madrid Conference in October 1991. This was the first time the parties sat face to face at the same table. The conference did not produce an agreement immediately but paved the way for later negotiations, such as the Oslo Accords (1993) and the Israel-Jordan peace treaty (1994).

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: The Aswan High Dam on the Nile River, completed in 1970, was built with financial and technical assistance from which country?
giai_thich: After the US and Britain withdrew their loan in 1956, the Soviet Union helped Egypt build the dam. The dam controls the annual flooding of the Nile, provides electricity and irrigation water, and created Lake Nasser, one of the largest artificial lakes in the world. Many ancient temples, such as Abu Simbel, had to be cut into blocks and relocated to avoid flooding.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which year did Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Egyptian President Anwar Sadat jointly receive the Nobel Peace Prize?
giai_thich: The two leaders were awarded the prize in 1978, shortly after the Camp David Accords and before the official peace treaty was signed in 1979. Begin had been the leader of an underground armed group during the British mandate, while Sadat had launched a war in 1973, so their reconciliation surprised the world. 1993 was the year the Oslo Accords were signed.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In 1952, which group of officers overthrew King Farouk of Egypt?
giai_thich: The Free Officers Movement was secretly organized by Gamal Abdel Nasser, with General Muhammad Naguib as the nominal leader. On July 23, 1952, they staged a coup with almost no bloodshed, and King Farouk fled the country on a yacht. In 1953, Egypt became a republic. July 23 is Egypt's National Day.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: Who was the leader of the 1919 revolution in Egypt against British rule?
giai_thich: Saad Zaghloul led a delegation (wafd) that wanted to attend the Paris Peace Conference to demand independence for Egypt but was arrested by the British and exiled to Malta. This sparked a revolution involving all classes, both Muslims and Christians, including women. In 1922, Britain granted limited independence to Egypt, and the Wafd Party became the largest party.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: In which battle in 1882 was Colonel Ahmed Urabi's uprising defeated by British forces?
giai_thich: Ahmed Urabi was an Egyptian officer of peasant origin who opposed the dominance of Turkish officials and Europeans. In September 1882, British forces launched a surprise attack at dawn at Tel el-Kebir and defeated Urabi's troops in about an hour. Urabi was exiled to Ceylon (Sri Lanka). After this battle, the British occupied Egypt for over 70 years.

chu_de: History of Africa & the Middle East
cau_hoi: According to the 1899 treaty, Britain and Egypt established a "dual rule" over which territory?
giai_thich: After defeating the Mahdist state in 1898, Britain and Egypt established the "Anglo-Egyptian Sudan" regime, nominally ruled by both countries but effectively controlled by Britain. Sudan gained independence on January 1, 1956. Before South Sudan seceded in 2011, Sudan was the largest country in Africa.
